title: Maintaining an underground rainwater cistern
subtitle: Annual inspection, cleaning, and filter maintenance for below-ground storage tanks
excerpt: An underground rainwater cistern stores thousands of litres and demands little attention compared with above-ground water butts, but it is not maintenance-free. Sediment accumulates at the base, the first-flush diverter needs periodic draining, and the inlet filter must be cleared to maintain flow. An annual inspection prevents the build-up of problems that are expensive to fix.
sourceNotes: CIRIA C539 Rainwater and Greywater Use in Buildings. Rainharvesting Systems (Graf, Wisi) installation and maintenance manuals 2024. British Standard BS 8515:2023 on rainwater harvesting.

glossaryTerms.definition: An inlet fitting that disperses incoming water along the base of the cistern without disturbing settled sediment. Ensures fine particles settle and stay settled rather than being re-suspended with each inflow event.

A suction device that draws water from just below the surface of the cistern, where water is clearest, rather than from the potentially turbid base. Supplied as standard on most residential underground cistern systems.

content.text: An underground cistern slowly builds up fine sediment: particles from tiles, pollen, and organic debris that gets through the inlet filter. The sediment settles to the base and only reaches the pump when the water level drops very low. A good system with a
and a floating suction filter keeps the drawn water clear all year. The maintenance task is to keep the inlet filter clear, check the sediment level once a year, and clean when needed.

Inspect the inlet filter (usually located in the downpipe run or at the cistern inlet lid). Clear any accumulated debris with a stiff brush and running water. Cracked or torn filter mesh should be replaced, the filter is the last defence before debris enters the cistern.

Check the overflow. The overflow pipe routes excess water away when the cistern is full. Clear any blockages at the outlet end, a blocked overflow causes the cistern to overflow around the access lid, potentially waterlogging the surrounding ground.
Open the access lid and inspect the
. Check that the floating filter is buoyant and that the suction hose is connected and unkinked. A floating filter that has sunk to the base is drawing from the sediment zone.

Inspect the water surface. Clear water with no smell indicates the system is working normally. A sulphurous smell from an open cistern that is full suggests stagnation, either the cistern is not cycling (the pump has not been used and rainwater has not been replenishing it), or the calmed inlet is missing and sediment is being re-suspended.

When sediment depth at the cistern base exceeds about 100 mm (visible from the access hatch with a torch), it should be removed. The method depends on whether the cistern has a sump access port. For small tanks (up to 3,000 litres) with a large access hatch, lower a vacuum pump or sludge pump on a hose to the base and extract into a garden waste bucket. The sediment is excellent garden compost material, fine mineral particles and partially degraded organic matter. Allow the tank to refill to at least 50% before resuming pump use; running the pump dry damages the impeller.

A hydrogen sulphide smell (rotten egg) from an underground cistern indicates anaerobic decomposition in the sediment layer. This usually means the pump has not been used for several months and the water has stagnated. Pump out half the water, refill from the mains if available, and allow fresh rainwater to replenish the balance. If the smell returns within two weeks, desludge the cistern.
